# Virginia UAS Regulatory Summary

**Prepared for:** Commercial AEC consultants conducting UAS-supported work in Virginia  
**Research date:** 2026-08-02  
**Version:** 2.0 (Phase 2 — practical interpretation complete)
**Model / checkpoint:** Objective research model retained from Phase 1; Phase 2 interpretations drafted with OpenAI GPT-5 (Codex; exact checkpoint unavailable)
**Interpretation scope:** Agent Instructions v6 (August 2, 2026)
**Scope note:** Statewide and state-agency authorities only. Municipal, county, tribal, federal, land-manager-specific federal, property-specific, site-specific, and live-airspace requirements are outside this summary.

> **Process note:** Objective research is retained from the Phase 1 source packet. The four practical-interpretation roles were completed in Phase 2 on 2026-08-02 using OpenAI GPT-5 (Codex; exact checkpoint unavailable).

## 1. State overview

Virginia preempts most political-subdivision regulation of privately owned UAS, but permits takeoff-and-landing rules on subdivision-owned property under Virginia Aviation Board procedures and exceptions. State criminal provisions address operations near dwellings after notice or for harassment, federal UAS security restrictions, correctional facilities, utilities and critical infrastructure, contracted defense facilities, privacy-sensitive peeping, and specified protected persons. State law also limits investigative UAS use by public bodies while preserving non-law-enforcement government missions and private commercial use.

Property-use rules are important for field planning. Virginia State Parks prohibit voluntary landing or unlawful operation within a park. Department of Wildlife Resources rules prohibit unauthorized use on department-owned lands as well as drone hunting and wildlife harassment. Unmanned aircraft are exempt from Virginia aircraft registration. No enacted general manufacturer or country-of-origin restriction was located; the current UAS procurement limitation is confined to weaponized aircraft acquired by specified public agencies.

## 2. Statewide laws

### VA-001 — Residential proximity, harassment, and notice to desist

**Authority:** Va. Code § 18.2-121.3(A)(i), (C)  
**Status:** Current / in force

Section 18.2-121.3 makes it a Class 1 misdemeanor to knowingly and intentionally cause a UAS to enter another's property and come within 50 feet of a dwelling house either to coerce, intimidate, or harass another person, or after actual notice to desist for any other reason. Subsection C states exceptions involving consent, federally authorized and otherwise lawful operation consistent with federal regulations, employee official business, and specified utility or facility employees. The provision requires the stated intent, proximity, property-entry, or notice elements; it is not written as a general statewide setback from every dwelling.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Use a mission-specific collection plan for Statewide; another person's property within 50 feet of a dwelling house that limits camera angle, dwell time, audio, zoom, thermal capture, and retention to the contracted purpose. Brief the crew on aborting or redirecting collection when people, residences, or unrelated activity enter the sensor footprint.
- **Agency Practitioner:** N/A — no agency process involved
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under Va. Code § 18.2-121.3(A)(i), (C); a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.

### VA-002 — Federal UAS security restrictions and correctional facilities

**Authority:** Va. Code § 18.2-121.3(A)(ii)–(iii), (C)  
**Status:** Current / in force

Section 18.2-121.3 makes it a Class 1 misdemeanor to knowingly and intentionally cause a UAS to take off or land in violation of current FAA Special Security Instructions or UAS Security Sensitive Airspace Restrictions. It also covers dropping any item within a state or local correctional facility or juvenile correctional center, and obtaining a still or video image of an identifiable inmate or resident there. Subsection C contains consent, federally authorized operation, employee-business, and specified facility-employee exceptions, subject to their exact terms.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Treat written facility coordination as a pre-mobilization gate for work within Statewide; FAA security-restricted launch and landing locations and state or local correctional facilities or juvenile correctional centers; do not rely only on flight-app geofencing or a client's general site-access instruction. Include lost-link, return-to-home, emergency landing, sensor-direction, and observer controls that prevent an unintended facility overflight, prohibited capture, loitering, or interference.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Use the current named facility or administering agency application or request channel and provide the mission description, dates, aircraft, pilot, and requested operating area. The packet identifies the approval as: Consent or another subsection C exception may be material; federal authorization may also be required. Because the verified source does not establish a dependable review time for every case, confirm completeness, reviewer, lead time, approval duration, and field-contact expectations directly with the agency.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Use configuration-controlled payload interfaces and maintain documentation showing the purpose, operating limits, release safeguards, aircraft weight, and approved mission configuration. Avoid buying or fielding attachments whose capability could place an otherwise ordinary mapping aircraft within a weapon, projectile, contraband-delivery, or regulated dispensing provision.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under Va. Code § 18.2-121.3(A)(ii)–(iii), (C); a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.

### VA-003 — Utilities, critical infrastructure, and maritime-security facilities

**Authority:** Va. Code § 18.2-121.3(B)–(C)  
**Status:** Current / in force; subsection B amended in 2025

Subsection B makes it a Class 4 felony to knowingly, intentionally, and without authorization cause a UAS to enter the airspace over public services or utilities described in § 18.2-162, federally defined critical infrastructure including Department of Defense-authorized military bases, or a facility covered by the Maritime Transportation Security Act. Subsection C provides exceptions for consent, federal authorization coupled with otherwise lawful operation consistent with federal regulations, employee official business, and specified utility, infrastructure, or facility employees conducting official business.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Treat written facility coordination as a pre-mobilization gate for work within Airspace over covered utilities, critical infrastructure, military bases, and Maritime Transportation Security Act facilities; do not rely only on flight-app geofencing or a client's general site-access instruction. Include lost-link, return-to-home, emergency landing, sensor-direction, and observer controls that prevent an unintended facility overflight, prohibited capture, loitering, or interference.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Use the current named facility or administering agency application or request channel and provide the mission description, dates, aircraft, pilot, and requested operating area. The packet identifies the approval as: Authorization, consent, federal compliance, or covered official-business status may be material. Because the verified source does not establish a dependable review time for every case, confirm completeness, reviewer, lead time, approval duration, and field-contact expectations directly with the agency.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under Va. Code § 18.2-121.3(B)–(C); a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.

### VA-004 — Contracted defense facilities and controlled technical information

**Authority:** Va. Code § 18.2-121.3(D)  
**Status:** Current / in force; effective July 1, 2025

Subsection D makes it a Class 4 felony to knowingly, intentionally, and without authorization cause a UAS to enter a contracted defense facility's property and obtain or attempt to obtain imagery containing or revealing controlled technical information. This rule applies notwithstanding subsections A–C. The statute defines a contracted defense facility by specified Department of Defense contract work and defines controlled technical information by reference to DFARS clause 252.204-7012, excluding lawfully public information. It also gives qualifying facility owners, operators, and employees limited immunity for certain defensive actions that do not injure a person.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Treat the applicable written consent or authorization under Va. Code § 18.2-121.3(D) as a pre-mobilization gate and ensure it covers the site, dates, aircraft, crew, payload, and purpose. Do not lock the field schedule until the approving person and any notice, boundary, insurance, or operating conditions are documented.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Use the current named facility or administering agency application or request channel and provide the mission description, dates, aircraft, pilot, and requested operating area. The packet identifies the approval as: Facility authorization is material; no general state permit is stated. Because the verified source does not establish a dependable review time for every case, confirm completeness, reviewer, lead time, approval duration, and field-contact expectations directly with the agency.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under Va. Code § 18.2-121.3(D); a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.

### VA-005 — UAS peeping or spying into dwellings

**Authority:** Va. Code § 18.2-130.1(B)–(C)  
**Status:** Current / in force

Section 18.2-130.1 makes it unlawful to knowingly and intentionally cause a UAS to secretly or furtively peep or spy, or attempt to peep or spy, into or through an opening of a building, structure, or enclosure occupied or intended as a dwelling. The conduct must be without just cause and occur under circumstances violating the occupant's reasonable expectation of privacy. A violation is a Class 1 misdemeanor. The section does not apply to a lawful criminal investigation.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Use a mission-specific collection plan for Statewide; buildings, structures, or enclosures occupied or intended as dwellings that limits camera angle, dwell time, audio, zoom, thermal capture, and retention to the contracted purpose. Brief the crew on aborting or redirecting collection when people, residences, or unrelated activity enter the sensor footprint.
- **Agency Practitioner:** N/A — no agency process involved
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Treat Peeping or spying into a dwelling with a UAS as a documented stop-work or redesign trigger because the packet identifies criminal, civil, evidentiary, or damage exposure. The contract and flight record should preserve the site screening, authority or exception relied upon, crew briefing, and incident/escalation path; obtain counsel where the facts sit near an undefined boundary or intent element.

### VA-006 — Status-specific following, contact, and imaging restrictions

**Authority:** Va. Code § 18.2-324.2  
**Status:** Current / in force

Section 18.2-324.2 prohibits a person required to register under § 9.1-901 from knowingly and intentionally using a UAS to follow or contact another person without permission, or to capture recognizable images of another person without permission. It separately prohibits a respondent under specified protective orders from knowingly and intentionally using a UAS to follow, contact, or capture images of the petitioner or another individual named in the order. Either violation is a Class 1 misdemeanor. These are status-specific operator restrictions rather than general commercial UAS rules.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** This record has no routine effect on an AEC mission or ordinary fleet operation because it applies to a separately regulated person or activity. Do not treat it as a general UAS operating rule; address it only if the stated regulated-party condition is actually present.
- **Agency Practitioner:** N/A — no agency process involved
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under Va. Code § 18.2-324.2; a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.

### VA-007 — Public-body investigative use and weaponized public UAS

**Authority:** Va. Code § 19.2-60.1  
**Status:** Current / in force; amended in 2026

Section 19.2-60.1 generally requires a search, administrative, or inspection warrant when covered state or local bodies use UAS for criminal-law or regulatory investigations. It enumerates warrantless exceptions, including alerts, immediate danger, crash reconstruction, consent, certain arrest operations, investigation of UAS around government property or public critical infrastructure, and specified DEQ enforcement. Non-law-enforcement government support such as damage, traffic, flood, and wildfire assessment is outside the warrant requirement, and the section does not prohibit private commercial use. Public deployment or facilitation of weaponized UAS is generally prohibited, subject to stated exceptions.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** This record does not directly regulate an ordinary privately controlled AEC flight, but it can govern a mission performed for or integrated into the named public agency's program. Define in the scope and flight plan who authorizes the mission, controls the aircraft, receives the data, and is responsible for the cited records or use restrictions.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Use the current named facility or administering agency application or request channel and provide aircraft details. The packet identifies the approval as: Warrant or stated exception required for covered investigative use; no approval imposed on ordinary private commercial use. Because the verified source does not establish a dependable review time for every case, confirm completeness, reviewer, lead time, approval duration, and field-contact expectations directly with the agency.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Use configuration-controlled payload interfaces and maintain documentation showing the purpose, operating limits, release safeguards, aircraft weight, and approved mission configuration. Avoid buying or fielding attachments whose capability could place an otherwise ordinary mapping aircraft within a weapon, projectile, contraband-delivery, or regulated dispensing provision.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under Va. Code § 19.2-60.1; a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.

### VA-008 — Local preemption and subdivision-owned property

**Authority:** Va. Code § 15.2-926.3  
**Status:** Current / in force

Section 15.2-926.3 prohibits a political subdivision from regulating privately owned UAS use within its boundaries. A subdivision may regulate UAS takeoff and landing on property it owns, but the measure must follow Department of Aviation rules, be reported to the department, and be published through the statutory process. The section preserves access controls and enumerates protected operations, including federally compliant commercial operations, certain emergency or maintenance support, technical-malfunction landings, public-safety operations, and specified federal-government work.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Use the state rule to identify what a political subdivision may regulate, then check only the controlling property's published operating terms before launch. Record the applicable boundary, property owner, designated-use area, notice, and permission status in the flight packet without assuming that state preemption eliminates property-use conditions.
- **Agency Practitioner:** N/A — no agency process involved
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under Va. Code § 15.2-926.3; a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.

### VA-009 — State aircraft-registration exemption

**Authority:** Va. Code § 5.1-5(A)  
**Status:** Current / in force; amended in 2025

Virginia generally requires specified resident, based, aerial-application, and intrastate for-hire civil aircraft to register with the Department of Aviation before operation. Section 5.1-5(A), however, expressly states that an owner of an unmanned aircraft as defined in § 19.2-60.1 is not required to register that aircraft. This is an exemption from Virginia's aircraft-registration program, not an exemption from applicable federal registration, FAA operating requirements, property-use restrictions, or the other state UAS provisions summarized here.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Do not add a Virginia aircraft-registration task for the unmanned aircraft covered by this express exemption. Keep the exemption citation with the fleet compliance record while continuing to screen for mission-specific property, facility, wildlife, and client requirements.
- **Agency Practitioner:** N/A — no agency process involved
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Do not create a state-registration purchasing gate where this record expressly exempts unmanned aircraft. Keep federal registration and asset records current, and separately check whether a mission-specific permit, property rule, weight threshold, or public-client specification still affects the selected system.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Preserve the mission screening and factual basis for compliance with Va. Code § 5.1-5(A), including the operating area, purpose, approvals, and any relied-upon exception. Escalate ambiguous scope, conflicting client direction, or facts that could change the regulated party or activity before flight.

### VA-010 — Acquisition and use of weaponized UAVs by state agencies

**Authority:** Va. Code § 2.2-5515  
**Status:** Current / in force; public-agency rule

Section 2.2-5515 prohibits a Commonwealth agency or the leadership of an agency or department employing law-enforcement officers from acquiring or purchasing weaponized unmanned aerial vehicles and other listed military property. A covered agency that previously acquired a prohibited item may not use it without a Criminal Justice Services Board waiver based on good cause and a bona fide public-safety purpose; a request generally is limited to special-weapons or equivalent units, with a State Police exception. The Virginia National Guard and Virginia Defense Force are excluded.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** This record does not directly regulate an ordinary privately controlled AEC flight, but it can govern a mission performed for or integrated into the named public agency's program. Define in the scope and flight plan who authorizes the mission, controls the aircraft, receives the data, and is responsible for the cited records or use restrictions.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Use the current named facility or administering agency application or request channel and provide the mission description, dates, aircraft, pilot, and requested operating area. The packet identifies the approval as: Board waiver required for covered continued use; acquisition or purchase is prohibited. Because the verified source does not establish a dependable review time for every case, confirm completeness, reviewer, lead time, approval duration, and field-contact expectations directly with the agency.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Use configuration-controlled payload interfaces and maintain documentation showing the purpose, operating limits, release safeguards, aircraft weight, and approved mission configuration. Avoid buying or fielding attachments whose capability could place an otherwise ordinary mapping aircraft within a weapon, projectile, contraband-delivery, or regulated dispensing provision.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under Va. Code § 2.2-5515; a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.

### VA-011 — Attorney General interpretation of local zoning authority

**Authority:** Virginia Attorney General Opinion 22-046 (Jan. 6, 2023)  
**Status:** Current persuasive official interpretation

Opinion 22-046 concludes that Virginia law limits local authority over privately owned drones to regulation of takeoffs and landings on property owned by political subdivisions. It states that a locality therefore may not use zoning regulations to prohibit privately owned drone takeoffs and landings on private property or subject that activity to conditional- or special-use permit requirements. The opinion interprets § 15.2-926.3 and does not eliminate independent state law, federal aviation requirements, private property rights, or the subdivision-owned-property rules authorized by that section.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Use the state rule to identify what a political subdivision may regulate, then check only the controlling property's published operating terms before launch. Record the applicable boundary, property owner, designated-use area, notice, and permission status in the flight packet without assuming that state preemption eliminates property-use conditions.

## 3. State agency requirements and guidance

### VA-012 — Political-subdivision takeoff and landing regulations

**Authority:** 24VAC5-20-410 through 24VAC5-20-450  
**Status:** Current / in force; effective October 25, 2023

Virginia Aviation Board Part VIII permits political subdivisions to regulate UAS takeoff and landing on property they own. Rules may establish operating times and designate mapped properties presenting specific public-safety or natural-resource risks, where operators can be asked to demonstrate purpose and risk controls. Adoption requires Department of Aviation consistency review, public notice and hearing, reporting, and department publication before effectiveness. The regulation limits permits in designated-use areas, restricts rules for sub-0.55-pound aircraft, and preserves commercial, emergency, public-safety, governmental, and other stated exceptions.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Use the state rule to identify what a political subdivision may regulate, then check only the controlling property's published operating terms before launch. Record the applicable boundary, property owner, designated-use area, notice, and permission status in the flight packet without assuming that state preemption eliminates property-use conditions.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Use the current controlling political subdivision or property manager application or request channel and provide a location map, aircraft details. The packet identifies the approval as: Site-specific information or permission may be required on mapped increased-concern property; no permit in designated-use areas except as stated. Because the verified source does not establish a dependable review time for every case, confirm completeness, reviewer, lead time, approval duration, and field-contact expectations directly with the agency.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under 24VAC5-20-410 through 24VAC5-20-450; a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.

### VA-013 — Virginia State Parks aviation rule

**Authority:** 4VAC5-30-400  
**Status:** Current / in force

Virginia's State Parks aviation rule provides that no person may voluntarily land or unlawfully operate within or upon a park an airplane, remote-control model aircraft, helicopter, unmanned aerial system, drone, balloon, parachute, or other aviation apparatus. “Voluntarily” means anything other than a forced landing. Rescue and evacuation aircraft are exempt for emergencies and approved training exercises. The rule does not state a general commercial UAS permit or waiver process, and DCR's current public guidance describes drones as not flyable in state parks under this provision.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Confirm the controlling land unit and current property-use rule for All parks, recreational areas, parkways, historical and natural areas, natural area preserves, sites, and other DCR-managed areas covered by Chapter 30 before selecting launch and recovery points. Record the boundary and any closures or site conditions in the flight packet rather than relying on a general statewide assumption.
- **Agency Practitioner:** N/A — no agency process involved
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Identify whether the cited material is incorporated into the contract, permit, property-use approval, or agency standard before describing it as mandatory. Where it is not binding, record any deliberate deviation and the equivalent risk control or technical basis accepted by the client.

### VA-014 — Wildlife and Department of Wildlife Resources lands

**Authority:** 4VAC15-20-240  
**Status:** Current / in force

Except as authorized by the DWR director or designee, 4VAC15-20-240 prohibits using a drone or unmanned aircraft to hunt, take, kill, drive, or herd wild animals for hunting or trapping; to harass wildlife by significantly disrupting normal behavior; or on department-owned lands. It also prohibits hunting or assisting a hunt on the same calendar day on property after using a drone to locate or surveil wildlife during an open season. The rule preserves department-authorized wildlife management and specified federal or animal-control activities, and allows certain department employees, contractors, or agents acting for approved needs.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Screen the mission for active hunting and wildlife sensitivity within Statewide wildlife activity and department-owned lands; plan altitude, stand-off distance, route, observers, and abort criteria to avoid pursuit, harassment, or assistance to a taking. Document the project's environmental or infrastructure purpose and pause if animals materially react to the aircraft.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Use the current Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources application or request channel and provide aircraft details. The packet identifies the approval as: Director or designee authorization is required for otherwise prohibited use. Because the verified source does not establish a dependable review time for every case, confirm completeness, reviewer, lead time, approval duration, and field-contact expectations directly with the agency.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under 4VAC15-20-240; a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.

## 4. Non-Regulatory Context

The 2025 General Assembly considered HB 2038, which would have restricted public-body procurement and use of defined insecure UAS and directed development of state cybersecurity certification and approved-model lists. The bill was left in House General Laws and did not become current law. It is included here only as a future-update signal, not as an operative requirement.

## 5. Unresolved questions

1. **State parks:** What written authorization, if any, will DCR use for a nonemergency state project or contractor mission within a park, and does the answer vary by park or project sponsor?
2. **DWR lands:** What information, lead time, and approval instrument does the director or designee require for an AEC mission on department-owned land?
3. **Subdivision-owned launch sites:** Which current local property rules are published in the Department of Aviation inventory, and what mapped safety or natural-resource conditions apply to the proposed site?
4. **Protected facilities:** Does the planned imagery reveal controlled technical information, or does the project cross property or airspace described in § 18.2-121.3(B) or (D)?
5. **Procurement:** Will a successor to failed HB 2038 create manufacturer, component, country-of-origin, cybersecurity, public-contract, or fleet-replacement restrictions?
